slides.title: How information retrieval evolved over time?
slides.body:
![[fig-ir-history-convergence|85%]]

***

| **1950** | **1990** | **2010** | **2020** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Retrieve records** | **Rank documents** | **Learn representations** | **Generate responses** |
| Boolean retrieval | BM25, PageRank | [word2vec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), BERT | RAG, generative search |

***

- Is generative AI part of information retrieval?
- **What exactly is IR in 2026?**
slides.notes: Information retrieval began as matching queries to records, then became ranking at web scale, then representation learning. In the 2020s, systems increasingly retrieve evidence and generate the response, making the system boundary harder to draw. This deck asks what should still count as IR in 2026; if short on time, skip the individual historical examples.
slides.summary: history of information retriaval ... and this deck will answer what is IR in 2026? - is genAI used in IR?

slides.title: History of Search, Recommender systems and Conversational AI
slides.body:
<!-- gap -->

| Lineage | Selected papers | Signal added | Scope in cited work |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Classical information retrieval** | [Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309); Salton, **1968**; [Salton et al., 1975](https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220); [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) | Term frequency, inverse document frequency, document length | Lexical document–query ranking; no link graph or user model |
| **Web search** | [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/); [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140) | Link structure as authority and hub signals | Ranking web pages from content and links, not individual preferences or dialogue |
| **Recommender systems** | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905); [Amazon item-to-item filtering, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344); [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) | Ratings, purchases, and user–item interactions | Interaction-based prediction; [Schein et al., 2002](https://doi.org/10.1145/564376.564421) measured the cold-start case |
| **Conversational interfaces** | [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) | Scripts, learned sequence context, attention, then retrieved evidence | ELIZA matched scripted patterns; seq2seq and Transformer generated from learned context; RAG coupled generation to retrieval |

***

> The cited sequence adds term statistics (**1957–1975**), links (**1998–1999**), user–item behavior (**1994–2009**), learned sequence context (**2014–2017**), and retrieval-grounded generation (**2020**).
slides.notes: Salton’s 1968 model established the core abstraction—represent documents and queries as vectors—but similarity remained lexical and context-free. Search, recommendation, and conversation then evolved separately because each optimized a different signal and objective; learned embeddings later gave them shared representational machinery. If short on time, omit the intermediate conversational milestones but retain Salton’s limitations and the four-signal summary.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Cite Salton 1968 vector space model limitations.

slides.title: Four histories converge on one operation: rank
slides.body:
![[fig-four-lineages-to-rank|68%]]

*Figure 1. Milestones that changed what could be scored—and therefore ranked.*

| Lineage | From → to | Ranking signal |
|---|---|---|
| **IR** | [Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309) → [Salton et al., 1975](https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220) → [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) | term frequency → vector similarity → probabilistic relevance |
| **Web search** | [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) → [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140) | link authority and hub structure |
| **Recommenders** | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905) → [Amazon, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344) → [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) | neighbour agreement → item similarity → latent preference |
| **Conversation** | [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) | rules → sequence likelihood → attention → retrieved evidence |

> The interfaces changed; selecting and ordering the next best item remained the common problem.
slides.notes: Figure 1 links each lineage’s canonical citations to the signal used for ranking. IR ranked documents, web search added authority, recommenders ranked items for a person, and conversational systems eventually ranked both evidence and responses. If short on time, skip the intermediate milestones and emphasize the convergence on selection and ordering.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Show Figure 1 linking citations to rank.

slides.title: The ranked object changed; the accuracy question did not
slides.body:
- **IR:** term statistics ([Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309)) → vector space ([Salton et al., 1975](https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220)) → [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/)
- **Web search:** documents → link authority with [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) and [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140)
- **Recommendation:** user neighborhoods ([GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905)) → item similarity ([Amazon, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344)) → [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263)
- **Conversation:** [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401)

***

| Accuracy condition | User-based CF | Item-based CF |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence used | Ratings from nearest users | Co-consumption among nearest items |
| Stronger when | User overlap is dense and preferences persist | Item relationships are dense and stable |
| Main accuracy loss | Sparse or rapidly changing user profiles | New or rarely consumed items |
| Reference system | GroupLens | Amazon item-to-item CF |
| Fair comparison | Same temporal split and Precision@k, Recall@k or NDCG@k | Same temporal split and metric |

> There is no dataset-independent winner: accuracy follows the stability of the neighborhood.
slides.notes: The historical shift is from ranking documents, to pages, to items, to generated responses; each lineage changes the candidate set but retains ranking. User-based versus item-based accuracy cannot be reduced to one universal number because results depend on sparsity, time split and metric; Amazon’s contribution was also about making item relationships practical to precompute. If short on time, read only the recommendation row and the final sentence.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Table comparing user-based versus item-based accuracy.

slides.title: Before 2018, four ranking lineages remained separate
slides.body:
| Lineage | Historical shift | Ranked object |
|---|---|---|
| **Information retrieval** | term counts → vector similarity → [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) | documents for a query |
| **Web search** | text relevance → link authority via [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) and [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140) | web pages |
| **Recommenders** | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905) → item-to-item [Amazon, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344) → [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) | items for a user |
| **Conversation** | [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) | responses or actions |

***

**Siri and Alexa exposed the isolation**

`speech recognition → intent classifier → domain/skill router → API or search → response template → speech synthesis`

Separate models, indexes and teams met through routed APIs—not a shared semantic representation.

> The operation was already shared—ranking—but the architecture was not.
slides.notes: IR, web search, recommendation and conversation all learned to score candidates, but they optimized different objects and maintained separate data and serving stacks. Siri and Alexa are shown schematically because their production architectures are proprietary; the important point is the explicit routing between speech, intent, skills, search and response generation. If short on time, skip the chronology inside each row and land on the architectural isolation.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? List Siri and Alexa architecture isolation.

slides.title: 2018: BERT made one language model useful across retrieval and dialogue
slides.body:
![[fig-bert-convergence|76%]]

| Before 2018 | Shared shift after the [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) |
|---|---|
| **IR/search:** lexical matching and link signals | Contextual representations for query–document relevance |
| **Recommenders:** collaborative signals and matrix factorization | Text, users and items represented in learned embedding spaces |
| **Conversation:** task-specific pipelines | Pretrained language models adapted to intent and response tasks |

**BERT result:** 80.5 GLUE score—**+7.7 points** over the previous best—and 93.2 F1 on SQuAD 1.1 (**+1.5**) ([Devlin et al., 2018](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)).

> The interfaces remained distinct; pretrained language representations became their common substrate.
slides.notes: BERT did not yet unify complete search, recommendation and conversational systems, but it changed their shared technical foundation: pretrain once, then fine-tune by task. The reported gains established contextual Transformer representations as a practical replacement for many task-specific language pipelines. If short on time, state only the GLUE gain and the distinction between shared substrate and still-separate products.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Cite Devlin et al 2018 performance gain.

slides.title: Four histories converged on one architecture
slides.body:
| Lineage | Independent foundations | Path into convergence |
|---|---|---|
| **Information retrieval** | [Luhn, 1957](https://doi.org/10.1147/rd.14.0309) → [Salton et al., 1975](https://doi.org/10.1145/361219.361220) → [BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) | lexical retrieval + learned representations |
| **Web search** | [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) + [HITS, 1999](https://doi.org/10.1145/324133.324140) | link, content and user signals in one ranker |
| **Recommenders** | [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905) → [Amazon, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344) → [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) | sequence models combine items, context and intent |
| **Conversation** | [ELIZA, 1966](https://doi.org/10.1145/365153.365168) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) | [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) + [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) |

<!-- gap -->

## ≈90%
**Working estimate for new systems using Transformer-based components across retrieval, recommendation or dialogue.**  
*Not an audited industry statistic; prevalence varies by workload and deployment cost.*

> The interfaces remain distinct; the representation and ranking machinery no longer does.
slides.notes: The historical pattern is separation followed by architectural convergence: statistical retrieval, graph authority, collaborative filtering and dialogue each supplied a different signal. The 90% figure is explicitly a keynote estimate, not a measured census; the defensible claim is that Transformer components now dominate newly designed systems while BM25, graph features and matrix methods remain in production. If short on time, read only the final column and state the qualification on the estimate.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Claim 90 percent of new systems use transformers.

slides.title: 2010–2024: four architectures converged on a shared core
slides.body:
![[fig-architecture-overlap-2010-2024]]

**Figure 2 · Architecture overlap, 2010–2024**
Separate IR, search, recommendation and conversation stacks increasingly share representations, retrieval, ranking and generation.

[Matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263) → [seq2seq, 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215) → [Transformer, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) → BERT, 2018 → [RAG, 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) → shared LLM stack, 2023

> The architecture converged before the user signals did.
slides.notes: Figure 2 traces architectural overlap rather than claiming that the four products became identical: their objectives, evaluation and interfaces remain distinct. The inflection points are seq2seq, the Transformer, BERT and RAG, culminating in the shared LLM stack by 2023–2024. If short on time, state only the distinction between a shared architecture and still-separate user signals.
slides.summary: answers: How has the historical development of IR, search, recommender systems and conversational interfaces? Display Figure 2 plotting architecture overlap from 2010 to 2024.

slides.title: Search became a personalized retrieval problem
slides.body:
**Global rank**
[BM25, 1994](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/) + [PageRank, 1998](https://research.google/pubs/the-anatomy-of-a-large-scale-hypertextual-web-search-engine/) rank documents from query and link evidence

↓ **Interaction histories add a user signal** — [GroupLens, 1994](https://doi.org/10.1145/192844.192905) · [Amazon, 2003](https://doi.org/10.1109/MIC.2003.1167344) · [matrix factorization, 2009](https://doi.org/10.1109/MC.2009.263)

![[fig-shared-user-embedding-search-recsys|68%]]

| Shared space | Search | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| User vector **u** | combines **u** with query **q** | retrieves directly from **u** |
| Item vector **vᵢ** | reranks query candidates | ranks candidate items |
| Core signal | lexical + authority + **u·vᵢ** | context + **u·vᵢ** |

> Search and recommendation differ in the request—not in the representation.
slides.notes: The architectural convergence is a shared user–item embedding space: search adds an explicit query, while recommendation often infers intent from the user and context. BM25 and PageRank remain useful signals; personalization augments rather than replaces them. If short on time, skip the chronology and explain only the two paths through the diagram.
